title: Off Broadway Review: SMALL - Bored and Confused?
transcript: Hello and welcome to Board and Confused, where I review shows based on two criteria. One, was I bored? Two, was I confused? Today's show is Small, playing right now at the Pershing Square Signature Center Theater here in New York City. Now, this is a one-person show written and performed by Robert Montano and directed by Jesse D. Hill. But before I get into this, please take a moment to like, comment, and subscribe. It really helps me grow this channel and get press tickets to see shows like Small. So, what did I know going into Small? Well, true to form, I knew almost nothing. I purposely avoid reading about shows before I see them. And I didn't even register that the playbill has an image of a horse faded in the background right there on the cover. And still, I walked in completely blank on what the show was about. That is how committed I am to knowing nothing. What I did do, as I like to do, was read the author's note in the program, where Montano thanks his mother for taking him to Belmont Park for the first time, his father, and Chita Rivera. And I thought, "Okay, a horse, Chita Rivera, this guy is going to take an interesting route to becoming a dancer." So, let's talk about how the show came to be. The show premiered back in March of 2022 at the Penguin Rep Theater in Hudson Valley. And from what I understand, it was the legendary Chita Rivera herself who helped Montano get that initial production off the ground. She used her industry connections to champion the project, eventually coming on board as part of the producing team for its off-Broadway debut at 59 East 59th Street Theaters in 2023. That run generated some serious buzz. The show earned nominations for the Drama Desk Award and the Outer Critics Circle Award for Outstanding Solo Performance in 2024. It also picked up the Arts Council of Rockland Award. After that, it hit the road playing venues across the country, and now it has returned to New York City for what I think is its most prominent engagement yet, a limited run at Signature Theatre, running through July 25th, 2026. So, this is a show that has been building and building, and you can feel that in the performance. This is a piece that has been rehearsed, road tested, and refined. So, what is Small actually about? Well, Small is a true autobiographical story about Robert Montano growing up in Hempstead, Long Island, right near Belmont Park, and falling absolutely, obsessively in love with horse racing. As a small kid, he's drawn to jockeys the way other kids are drawn to baseball players or rock stars. And through sheer force of will and personality, he manages to ingratiate himself into the world of Belmont Park, eventually getting mentored by jockey Robert Pineda and pursuing a real career as a jockey. But, here's the thing. Nature had other plans. He started growing and growing, and he ended up at 5'8", which I can tell you, as someone who stands 5'8 and 3/4 of an inch, is not super small. He is fighting his own body the entire time. He's not eating, he's purging, taking drugs, extreme dehydration, all to meet the strict weight requirements. And he actually rode in seven races, but won none of them. His jockey career lasted about five months. The show is bookended by another love of his, dance. As a kid, he was obsessed with West Side Story and desperately wanted to play Bernardo, but fears he will never be tall enough. After leaving racing, he enrolls at Adelphi University's dance program, discovers he has a gift for it, and one week before graduating books his first Broadway show and professional dance job in Cats the Musical. He goes on to work with legends like Jerome Robbins, Rob Marshall, and Hal Prince and eventually lands the role he always dreamed of, Bernardo. The title Small refers both to what he needed to be as a jockey and to how he felt as a kid before dance gave him the stage to become as big as he wanted. All right, let's talk positives and negatives. On the positive side, and there are a lot of them, Robert Montano is a great performer. He plays around two dozen different characters in this show and he gives every single one a distinct physicality and a distinct vocal performance. And that's what's great about dancers, it what they bring to theater. They understand the importance of physicality. And Montano is emotionally connected in every moment and you never doubt that he lived every word of this story. The direction by Jesse D. Hill is also excellent. The staging is precise and kinetic. Every inch of the stage is used. There are moments where the lighting design by Jamie Roderick absolutely pops. The way they light the scale that he has to step on for his weigh-ins, focusing a pin light on his face, giving the feel of the different locations of the stables, Belmont Park, his parents' home, and the scenic design by Christopher and Justin Swader puts you right in the paddock. And sound design by Brian Ronan does all the rest. All of the technical elements are completely in service of the storytelling. This is a fully realized, professional, beautifully mounted production. The sequences involving the ticking clock, specifically when he has to be weighed in on the day of the race, this nightmare of having to lose 10 lb in 24 hours, these sequences are genuinely gripping. But, I do have concerns and my biggest one is structural and it's this. The show is bookended by two short sections about dance and about 90% of the play is about being a jockey and or his dream of being a jockey and achieving it. And because of this framing device which opens by telling you essentially that this guy is going to become a dancer, I spent much of the show waiting for the jockey part to end. I wasn't rooting for him to succeed as a jockey because I knew that wasn't going to be ultimately where he ended up. I was rooting for him to give it up and find his love of dance. And that created a strange emotional tension that for me was working against the play. And I want to be clear, the story is very interesting and he tells it beautifully. But you haven't given me a character I can really root for. Bobby is likeable but Bobby is a teenager and he thinks he knows what he wants but as an audience we can clearly see that this dream isn't for him. I also found large portions of it deeply uncomfortable, the self-harm, the purging, the drug use. And it's all true but it's all in pursuit of a dream that is physically wrong for him. So watching a teenager destroy himself for a pipe dream is really hard to sit with, especially when the story has already told you how it ends. Other critics have praised the show as ripping, funny, sometimes shocking and they're not wrong but for me the shocking parts were less exciting and more just upsetting. That's a personal reaction but it's worth flagging if you're someone who is sensitive to these subjects. I also found an early section of the play when young Bobby first starts hanging around the stables to be a little overwhelming with all the new characters that were being introduced. He introduces what feels like five or six people in rapid succession and while each one is physically differentiated, it's a lot to track at once, especially when we are still getting our footing in the world of this show. So was I bored? Yes, I'll be honest, I got bored about 30 minutes into the show of this 100-minute show during those early stable scenes when Bobby is first getting his start and we're meeting all of these characters and watching him climb his way up the ladder, I found myself a little bit adrift because there wasn't a clear enough ticking clock yet. The dramatic question of will he become a jockey didn't grip me because the framing device had already told me the answer was sort of, but not really. But then, and this is important, the show turns a corner. Once his body starts working against him, once the weigh-ins become desperate, once he's taking pills to suppress his appetite, and we know the clock is running out, that's when I was really engaged. There's a scene where he has to lose 10 lb in 24 hours, and I thought that was a very gripping, probably the most gripping part of the play. So, it's not that the show is boring, it's just that the first act of the show took a while to find its stakes for me. Was I confused? Not really, no. This production is directed and designed so clearly that it's hard to get lost. Every transition feels purposeful, every beat lands, and I'll say I got a tiny bit turned around during those early stable scenes when he was introducing a lot of characters very quickly. I wasn't always sure who we were with or how important they'd be for the rest of the story, but that cleared up pretty quickly, and from that point on, I always knew exactly where I was in the show. So, to wrap this all up, Small is a very good piece of theater. The acting is great, the storytelling is impressive, the technical production is top-notch. Robert Montano is a genuine double threat. He is very clear in the show that singing is not a skill that he's getting hired for, but as an actor, dancer, telling his own story, he's fantastic. My lingering issue is a structural one. I never really found myself rooting for Bobby the jockey because I came in knowing Bobby the dancer was the real story. The the device that gives the show its emotional resolution, also for me drained some of the tension from the journey. But, that's a storytelling choice, not a failure of execution. Everything in the production is executed at very high level, and critics have largely agreed. The Wall Street Journal called it, quote, a gripping and vividly acted one-man show, end quote. And it's been praised across the board for the quality of the performance. The Drama Desk and the Outer Critics Circle nominations speak for themselves. This show has earned its reputation. So, who should go see Small? If you love one-person shows where a skilled physical performer really inhabits a whole world of characters, this is exactly what you want. If you're into stories about sports, grit, obsession, and second acts in life, this is also your show. And if you love good stagecraft, beautiful lighting, and a production that has been rehearsed and refined over 4 years, you will appreciate every bit of Small. And I'll say this personally, I knew almost nothing about horse racing going in, and I found the inside world of the Belmont Park stables genuinely fascinating. There's a whole culture there that I had zero exposure to, and I'm really glad I got to see it through Montano's eyes. If, on the other hand, you need your one-person shows to be primarily funny, this is not that show. It has humor, but it is not a comedy. And if you are sensitive to depictions of eating disorders, purging, and drug use, then but please know that those are present and portrayed realistically. I got a press ticket for this one, so thank you again to the press agent. As for where I sat, I was on the side towards the back, but I want to say at Signature Center's Alice Griffin Jewel Box Theater, it really does not matter where you sit. It is an intimate theater, the sightlines are great everywhere, and the production is is designed to fill the stage. So, don't stress about your seat. Where can you get your cheap tickets? I don't have specific discount info just yet, but I will post in the comments as soon as something becomes available. In the meantime, I check TodayTix for rush and lottery options. Small runs through July 25th, so you got some time this summer, but don't sleep on it. All right, that is my take on Small. I'm so glad I saw it, and I will see you at the next one. >> Don't want to drift away. Want to stay inside the play. Keep me engaged. Keep me amused with what's in front of me, CUZ I DON'T WANT to be bored and confused. >>
